KEY MESSAGE 1: Tranquil weather expected with above-average 
temperatures expected through Wednesday evening.

Current (2:00 PM EST) radar outlines light returns expanding 
along a line from UNV to FIG; however, observations at the 
airfields outline little (if any) precipitation falling at the 
sites. Given the low-level dry air in place, generally expect 
very little rainfall throughout the rest of the evening. If any 
rain is to fall, it will generally be light and not even enough 
to wet the ground, so have low PoPs in for this timeframe. This 
will begin a stretch of dry weather that is expected to continue
through Wednesday as a surface ridge works into the region. 
This will also supply the region with above-average temperatures
through Wednesday evening. The main weather concern will 
continue to be breezy winds through Wednesday given the low 
pressure system in western Quebec and high pressure across the 
Lower Ohio Valley bringing a tightening pressure gradient across
the region. Maximum wind gusts (30-40 mph across the highest 
elevations of the Laurels) will be occurring during the 
afternoon hours today and tomorrow.

KEY MESSAGE 2: Potential for the first accumulating snowfall of
the season, especially across the Laurels and the northern tier
of Pennsylvania.

The main focus of the forecast period will be the potential for
the first accumulating snowfall across portions of central 
Pennsylvania in the latter half of the week. Initially, chances 
for precipitation begin to ramp up Wednesday morning ahead of an
approaching low pressure system moves into the region from the 
Mid-Ohio Valley. Temperatures at onset are expected to be in the
mid-to-upper 30s across the northern tier and likely continue 
to trend warmer (even slightly) throughout the daytime. It is 
expected that temperatures will trend cooler after sunset; 
however, current forecast outlines lowest temperatures remaining
above freezing given the considerable cloud cover across the 
region. If anywhere is to observe some wet snowflakes overnight 
Wednesday night into Thursday, it would likely be across McKean 
County; however, confidence remains too low so have retained 
rain mentions in this forecast cycle.

All ensemble guidance points towards colder air working into 
the region Thursday night into Friday, which could bring the 
first accumulating snowfall to portions of central Pennsylvania.
During the daytime hours on Thursday, temperatures at 850mb 
range from +2 to +4C before trending closer to the -3C to -5C 
range, outlining the extent of cooler air is working into the 
region with this system. This will likely allow for a transition
to outright snow showers Thursday evening across portions of 
northwestern Pennsylvania and the Laurel Highlands where 
temperatures are expected to be much cooler than surrounding 
locations. Gradual mixing will likely continue into sunrise on 
Friday with areas generally north/west of the I-80/I-99 corridor
experiencing some potential for snow for the Friday morning 
commute. There remains a bit of uncertainty with respect to the 
daytime forecast of Friday with more recent NBM model guidance 
trending slightly cooler compared to previous runs. This has led
to a slight increase in the snowfall footprint compared to the 
previous forecast cycle. As this low pressure shifts further 
east, breezy northwesterly flow begins to take hold on the 
region late Friday and into Saturday which is expected to begin 
producing lake-enhanced snow showers downwind of the Great 
Lakes. Forecast could change with respect to this depending on 
the exact wind direction; however, additional snow showers will 
be possible for the first half of the weekend.

Given the set-up late Thursday through the first half of the 
weekend and the uncertainties still in play with respect to the 
snowfall/rain forecast, we urge folks to continue to monitor the
forecast. Given the signal for colder air in the region and 
given the climatology across the region, some portions of the 
area (most likely in the higher elevations of the Laurels and 
across the northern tier of Pennsylvania) are likely to see some
snowflakes with this approaching system. The first accumulating
snowfall across the region typically catches folks off guard, 
but keep in mind that we're getting into the middle of November 
where it will only become more likely that accumulating snowfall
will occur across the region. Take time to look over winter 
plans, whether it is for your home and/or car as we continue to 
transition into winter across the region.
